newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French markets react sharply to shock result.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French markets react sharply to shock result.

text.p: The French franc, stocks and bonds reacted sharply on Monday to an upset victory by the left in the first round of a parliamentary election, but prices steadied as domestic investors saw little scope for radical policy changes.
The stockmarket took the hardest hit, opening down nearly four percent as investors who had bet on a conservative victory ran for cover ahead of the runoff election on June 1.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index opened down 3.84 percent at 2,656.87 points but quickly came off its lows and was trading 3.31 percent lower at 2,673.13 at midday.

Shares in companies the current government plans to privatise but whose future could be affected by a possible left win in the parliamentary election fell sharpest. Traders said the market fears the state asset sales may be postponed on cancelled by a government of the Socialist and Communist parties.
The franc and bond prices slumped overnight but also steadied well above their lows in calm trading.

"The feeling, particularly in the bond market, is that the two major parties on the right and the left are committed to meeting the Maastricht criteria -- not in the strictest sense, but close enough to get in on the first round," said Merrill Lynch market strategist Joanne Perez said of the drive to meet this year's tough targets for joining the European single currency.
"So even if the Socialists get in, we don't expect a real increase in the deficit in the next year or two," she said.
Analysts cautioned that the French markets, the bourse in particular, would be volatile until the final vote next Sunday.
Many foreign investors were not expected to register their reaction to the first-round results until Tuesday, as Monday is a market holiday in both Britain and the United States.
"When the Americans wake up and see there may be Communists in the government, there'll be a second blow," said IFF Bourse trader Olivier Blitz.

With most votes counted, the Interior Ministry said on Monday that the Socialists, Communists and other left had polled 40.23 percent and the ruling RPR-UDF coalition and other right-wing candidates 36.51 percent. The far-right National Front scored 14.90 percent and ecologists scored 6.81 percent.
"There's nervousness because no one knows where we are. The polls were roughly right in terms of the share of the votes, but were totally wrong on the sharing of seats," a trader said.
The franc, which fell to 3.3755 to the German mark after the first projections on Sunday night putting the left ahead, sank further to 3.3773 but was steady around 3.3755 at midday.
A trader at a French bank said he did not expect the franc to fall much below 3.3825 on the view that the European single currency was unlikely to be derailed by a Socialist government.
"The only risk is that the foreigners will be wary of the Communists," he said.

June PIBOR futures opened 17 basis points lower at 96.30 and slumped as much as 34 basis points before climbing back to 96.27. The June bond futures contract, which dropped as low as 128, was trading at 128.46 at 1045 GMT.
The markets initially shuddered at the prospect of a "co-habitation" between conservative President Jacques Chirac and a government led by the Socialists and their Communist allies.

But traders said that after the initial knee-jerk reaction, cash-rich French domestic investors were stepping in to buy bonds along the curve at the higher yields, bringing the 10-year spread with Bunds back to minus 10, after touching minus three. The spread stood at minus 14 on Friday before the election.
"There's plenty of cash out there and they're going to have to buy come what may," said a trader at a French bank. "The political debate is almost a sideshow for many of these people."
The shock was biggest in the share market where the risk had not been priced in and where foreigners account for a bigger share of the activity.
"The stock market, putting its trust in opinion polls showing the right would win, had treated the election as a non-event. We are going to pay for it," said a stocks dealer.

Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney told Reuters Financial Television he expected a two-stage fall in the bourse, the initial disappointment on Monday and then further selling on Tuesday when foreign investors returned to the market.
Among the biggest losers, shares in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF were down 7.92 percent on concern that a Socialist-led government would try to block the privatisation.
Carmaker Renault's stock was down 5.13 percent on concerns its restructuring plans, entailing job losses, might also be held up by a government on the left.
